newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mozambique says privatisation central to reforms.
newsitem.headline: Mozambique says privatisation central to reforms.

text.p: The privatisation of state-owned enterprises is central to the Mozambique government's economic reform programme and is already delivering results, Prime Minister Pascoal Mocumbi said on Monday.
"Privatisation is a basic component of reactivating the national economy," he told a pan-African investment conference here.

Mozambique, enjoying an economic revival with the end of civil war which ravaged the country, is pursuing an ongoing privatisation programme involving the sale of around 700 state companies, including over 40 large ones.
Mocumbi said revenue collection was not the fundamental objective of the process. Rather the government hoped to revitalise key industries by improving management, technology and competitiveness.

The benefits were already being felt, he said. In the banking sector new private banks have opened, the Commercial Bank of Mozambique has been privatsied and plans are afoot to privatise the People's Development Bank.

These steps, together with the creation of an interbank foreign exchange market, have had a major impact on foreign exchange supply, contributing to the stability of the metical currency which depreciated by only five percent in 1996.

The private sector is also playing a growing role in the food industry following privatisation of state food concerns, contributing 95.8 percent of national food production in the first half of 1996 with the state making up just 4.2 percent.

Elsewhere, Cimentos de Mocambique, privatised in 1994, has seen sales rise by 73 percent a year. The group now supplies 80 percent of the national cement market, which totals 230,000 tonnes a year, compared with a market share of one-third when it was in state hands.
